findings.claim: The threat matrix's subprocess row constrains only WHERE subprocesses run (vault-root-bounded runner, argv-only, timeouts) and never establishes that the vault root itself is trusted. Combined with the resolution chain the candidate specifies, the vault root is a fully user/config-controlled directory whose scripts are then executed: design.md:17 (D5) resolves it from `--vault` > environment variable > an editable JSON registry row, and openspec/changes/longterm-mem/specs/longterm-mem-memory-access/spec.md:143-147 requires invoking 'the vault's retrieval entrypoint inside P's resolved vault'. No requirement in any added spec validates the vault directory's provenance, ownership, or script integrity before execution, so anyone who can write the registry file or set the vault environment variable in the agent's environment converts an ordinary `query`/`index`/`sync` call into arbitrary local code execution as the invoking user. Recommend an explicit requirement (trusted-root allowlist, ownership/mode check, or refusal of non-user-owned or world-writable vault roots) before the runner slice is authored.

findings.claim: The unified query contract specifies exactly one degrade path — vault not provisioned yields Engram-only results — and none for the mirror case. When the Engram side is unavailable (its SQLite file locked by the live WAL writer, missing, or busy) the design's contract turns that into a hard exit `engram_unavailable`, so the whole MCP `query` call fails even though the long-term vault tier is healthy and answerable. The same asymmetry applies to a vault subprocess failure: only the not-provisioned exit status is mapped to a status value, so a missing python3 or a failing retrieval script fails the call rather than degrading to Engram-only. Net production effect: a single-tier outage removes both tiers of memory from every agent session instead of degrading to the tier that still works.

findings.claim: The explicit promote surface is specified to reuse the page-emission, addressing and registration path only; index rebuild is bound exclusively to `sync`. An agent that calls the MCP `promote` tool and then immediately calls `query` will not find the page it just promoted, because the vault tier is answered by the BM25 index which nothing rebuilt. This is the same silent-invisibility failure the bridge probe recorded for the rejected export path (pages present on disk, zero chunks in the index, retrieval returning only pre-existing pages), reintroduced through the promote entrypoint rather than the export one.

findings.claim: The four named diagnostic checks cover vault-config resolvability, address-map integrity, wiki-registration consistency and runtime prerequisites, but none reports whether the retrieval index is current with respect to the promoted pages, and `status` reports only reachability, a boolean provisioning state, and a last-sync timestamp. After a rebuild step fails (the failure the rebuild requirement forces to be reported at the moment it happens) the pages remain on disk and unindexed, and from that point on every subsequent `status` and `doctor` run reports a provisioned vault and a healthy system while queries silently omit the newest canonical decisions. The condition has no operator-visible signal after the failing command's own output scrolls away.

findings.claim: Rollout and rollback are specified only for code (reverse-order revert, uninstall/purge); there is no failure-atomicity or resume contract for the promotion write itself, which mutates at least five separate artifacts per run — the page file, the vault address and source manifest, the master catalog, the append-only log, and the precedence sidecar — plus the sync-state record. A sync interrupted between those writes (crash, SIGINT, disk full, a subprocess timeout in the address allocation step) leaves the vault in a state no requirement defines: an address allocated but not recorded in the manifest, or a page written but absent from catalog and log. Because re-promotion is specified to reuse an existing address only when one is already recorded, the retry after such an interruption can allocate a second address and emit a duplicate page for the same observation, and the leftover inconsistency is only detectable, never repairable, through the doctor checks.

findings.claim: The design decision row and the task anchors give two different, non-interchangeable connection strings for the same read-only Engram handle: the design row uses bare query keys for the read-only pragma and the busy timeout, while the task anchors use the driver's pragma-parameter form and add a lock-mode key. Whichever form is not understood by the chosen driver is either rejected at open time or silently ignored, and the silent case is the damaging one: without the busy timeout actually applied, every read that lands while the live Engram writer holds the WAL write lock returns immediately as busy instead of waiting, surfacing as intermittent `engram_unavailable` failures on `query` and `sync` under exactly the concurrent conditions the design assumes (a running Engram server writing the same database). The read-only guarantee itself rests on the same unresolved key.

findings.claim: Local-edit precedence is defined entirely as a comparison against a sidecar store kept inside the vault, with no specified behavior when that store is absent, truncated, or unparseable — a realistic state given it lives beside vault content under the plugin's own auto-commit and can be lost by a vault restore, a revert, or an interrupted write. With no entries, every promoted page trivially satisfies the divergence condition, so the implementation must pick between two unspecified extremes: skip everything, turning every later sync into a permanent silent no-op while Engram and the vault drift apart, or treat the missing record as no divergence and overwrite, which is precisely the human-edit clobber this requirement exists to prevent. Naming the required behavior (rebuild-and-skip, or fail loud) removes the coin flip.

evidence: Inspected all 17 manifest paths in full from the supplied patch sections only; no working tree, index, or command access was used.

The candidate is documentation and specification only: 16 added markdown/JSON planning artifacts plus one rewritten roadmap mirror. No executable code, no test code, and no build or CI configuration is changed by this candidate, so no runtime regression can be introduced by it directly; reliability review therefore targets whether the specified behavior is provable as written.

Cross-read every requirement in the six new capability specs and the three delta specs against the design decision table, the slice/task plan, and the entry contract to find contradictions and unproved failure paths.

Confirmed positive coverage: idempotent reinstall, untagged-conflict refusal and byte-identical preservation are each given explicit scenarios per runtime in openspec/changes/longterm-mem/specs/longterm-mem-mcp-registration/spec.md, and the address allocate/reuse and catalog/log registration paths each carry a scenario in openspec/changes/longterm-mem/specs/longterm-mem-promotion/spec.md:92-128.

Findings concentrate on failure-path and boundary gaps: Engram-unreachable behavior is unspecified everywhere despite a dedicated exit code, only one vault subprocess exit code is mapped, the first-provision step has no failure scenario, and the interaction between local-edit precedence and the canon-wins status patch is unproved for a frontmatter-only human edit.

One internal contract contradiction is deterministic: the design decision table and the task anchors record two different read-only database connection strings for the same requirement, and the only assertion on that requirement cannot distinguish them.

The route-domain change is internally inconsistent about how many production parsers must learn the new route (proposal says two plus a test contract, the roadmap mirror says three, the task plan edits one Go production table plus the shell resolver), which leaves one of the route scenarios unprovable as written.

findings.claim: The threat matrix's subprocess row constrains only WHERE subprocesses run (vault-root-bounded runner, argv-only, timeouts) and never establishes that the vault root itself is trusted. Combined with the resolution chain the candidate specifies, the vault root is a fully user/config-controlled directory whose scripts are then executed: design.md:17 (D5) resolves it from `--vault` > environment variable > an editable JSON registry row, and openspec/changes/longterm-mem/specs/longterm-mem-memory-access/spec.md:143-147 requires invoking 'the vault's retrieval entrypoint inside P's resolved vault'. No requirement in any added spec validates the vault directory's provenance, ownership, or script integrity before execution, so anyone who can write the registry file or set the vault environment variable in the agent's environment converts an ordinary `query`/`index`/`sync` call into arbitrary local code execution as the invoking user. Recommend an explicit requirement (trusted-root allowlist, ownership/mode check, or refusal of non-user-owned or world-writable vault roots) before the runner slice is authored.

findings.claim: The unified query contract specifies exactly one degrade path — vault not provisioned yields Engram-only results — and none for the mirror case. When the Engram side is unavailable (its SQLite file locked by the live WAL writer, missing, or busy) the design's contract turns that into a hard exit `engram_unavailable`, so the whole MCP `query` call fails even though the long-term vault tier is healthy and answerable. The same asymmetry applies to a vault subprocess failure: only the not-provisioned exit status is mapped to a status value, so a missing python3 or a failing retrieval script fails the call rather than degrading to Engram-only. Net production effect: a single-tier outage removes both tiers of memory from every agent session instead of degrading to the tier that still works.

findings.claim: The explicit promote surface is specified to reuse the page-emission, addressing and registration path only; index rebuild is bound exclusively to `sync`. An agent that calls the MCP `promote` tool and then immediately calls `query` will not find the page it just promoted, because the vault tier is answered by the BM25 index which nothing rebuilt. This is the same silent-invisibility failure the bridge probe recorded for the rejected export path (pages present on disk, zero chunks in the index, retrieval returning only pre-existing pages), reintroduced through the promote entrypoint rather than the export one.

findings.claim: The four named diagnostic checks cover vault-config resolvability, address-map integrity, wiki-registration consistency and runtime prerequisites, but none reports whether the retrieval index is current with respect to the promoted pages, and `status` reports only reachability, a boolean provisioning state, and a last-sync timestamp. findings.claim: Rollout and rollback are specified only for code (reverse-order revert, uninstall/purge); there is no failure-atomicity or resume contract for the promotion write itself, which mutates at least five separate artifacts per run — the page file, the vault address and source manifest, the master catalog, the append-only log, and the precedence sidecar — plus the sync-state record. A sync interrupted between those writes (crash, SIGINT, disk full, a subprocess timeout in the address allocation step) leaves the vault in a state no requirement defines: an address allocated but not recorded in the manifest, or a page written but absent from catalog and log. Because re-promotion is specified to reuse an existing address only when one is already recorded, the retry after such an interruption can allocate a second address and emit a duplicate page for the same observation, and the leftover inconsistency is only detectable, never repairable, through the doctor checks.

findings.claim: The design decision row and the task anchors give two different, non-interchangeable connection strings for the same read-only Engram handle: the design row uses bare query keys for the read-only pragma and the busy timeout, while the task anchors use the driver's pragma-parameter form and add a lock-mode key. Whichever form is not understood by the chosen driver is either rejected at open time or silently ignored, and the silent case is the damaging one: without the busy timeout actually applied, every read that lands while the live Engram writer holds the WAL write lock returns immediately as busy instead of waiting, surfacing as intermittent `engram_unavailable` failures on `query` and `sync` under exactly the concurrent conditions the design assumes (a running Engram server writing the same database). The read-only guarantee itself rests on the same unresolved key.

findings.claim: Local-edit precedence is defined entirely as a comparison against a sidecar store kept inside the vault, with no specified behavior when that store is absent, truncated, or unparseable — a realistic state given it lives beside vault content under the plugin's own auto-commit and can be lost by a vault restore, a revert, or an interrupted write. With no entries, every promoted page trivially satisfies the divergence condition, so the implementation must pick between two unspecified extremes: skip everything, turning every later sync into a permanent silent no-op while Engram and the vault drift apart, or treat the missing record as no divergence and overwrite, which is precisely the human-edit clobber this requirement exists to prevent. Naming the required behavior (rebuild-and-skip, or fail loud) removes the coin flip.

findings.claim: The unrouted-row rejection is scoped by path prefix rather than by intent: only rows under the new component's directory are rejected when their route column is missing or unrecognized, while every other row keeps the silent default-to-skill behavior. An unrecognized route value on any other path is therefore still resolved to a skills destination without an error, which is the same misrouting failure this requirement exists to prevent, and no scenario covers an unrecognized route outside the guarded prefix.

openspec/changes/longterm-mem/specs/overlay-agent-route/spec.md:77-83 provides the only rejection scenario, also prefix-scoped

findings.claim: The no-residual-process scenario is stated as an assertion over the machine's process list, and the corresponding tasks implement it as an unchanged-process-list comparison plus a parent-scoped process lookup. Both are nondeterministic on a shared or containerized runner and platform-dependent, so the test will either flake or be skipped in the short mode the tasks themselves define, leaving the no-daemon property effectively unasserted in the default test run.
proof_refs: openspec/changes/longterm-mem/specs/longterm-mem-ops/spec.md:114-116 asserts over the process list after each subcommand
openspec/changes/longterm-mem/tasks.md marks both residual-process tests as skippable in short mode and relies on a parent-scoped process lookup
openspec/changes/longterm-mem/design.md:37 places the lifecycle checks in the short-mode-gated integration bucket

findings.claim: The linked-pair merge scenario depends on the promotion link between an Engram id and a vault page address, but the sidecar precedence store that holds that link is only introduced three slices later in the chained delivery order. At the slice where the scenario is proved, the join key must be faked, so the merge behavior is verified against a fixture shape that no earlier slice owns and no later slice re-verifies end to end.

openspec/changes/longterm-mem/entry.json:88-96 orders the mutability slice after the query merge slice

findings.claim: Three different requirements inside this one change all carry the identifier R-012 while tracing to three different upstream requirements, and the second scenario in this delta is vacuously true: a file that does not live under the skills directory is never enumerated by a skills-directory scan, so no implementation change can make that scenario fail. The duplicate identifiers make the change's traceability table ambiguous and the vacuous scenario contributes no evidence.
